Data Access and Retrieval

What if you need to access near-realtime data from a monitoring station? MATLAB can read and access data from a variety of online or cloud based locations with webread or wmsread.
% First Try This:
% What does the imported data look like?
tab = webread('https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/data/realtime2/RPLV2.txt');
% you can specify how you want webread to handle this data type with
% "options"
The readtable and readtimetable functions, however, have the built-in ability to read data from common tables/file types on the web. While webread is useful for its broad functionality, readtable is a more direct solution when we know our data is already in a table format.
% Newer, more direct functionality
tab = readtable('https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/data/realtime2/RPLV2.txt');
You may see a runtime warning about table headers. This warning lets you know that MATLAB has automatically modified a few column headers to put them into a valid MATLAB format (e.g., spaces replaced with underscores). Readtable has Name-Value argument pairs that let you specify if you want to preserve column headers, set rules for reading different data types, change text delimiters, and control over 60 other options for reading your data. Type help readtable in the command window to see more.
You can change the column headers interactively by double clicking their names in the variable editor window, or you can programmatically change multiple names at once.
tab.Properties.VariableNames

What if you realize after importing the data that you don't need all of the columns? You can once again choose to remove them interactively or programmatically. If you removevars interactively, you'll see the following command echo in your command window:
tab = removevars(tab, "TIDE");
MATLAB usually produces and shows the code for any manual or interactive actions you take. You can also use much of the same functionality on tables that you would use on matrices. For instance, you can also remove a variable - if you know which column it occupies - by running:
tab(:,ColumnNumber) = [];

Data Preprocessing

Creating Timetables
Before you analyze your data, you oftentimes have to preprocess it, cleaning up erroneous values or reformatting data. Let's combine the time, day, month, and year columns of our dataset into one column of datetime values.
% turn columns into datetime
t = [tab.year tab.month tab.day tab.hour tab.minute];
 
% MATLAB requires "seconds" if you're including "hours" and "minutes" in a
% datetime. We could create a "seconds" variable that's the same number of rows
% as the rest of the table. However, we can also simply add a column of 0's
% to our dates vector, t when converting to a datetime. Remember that you
% can operate in-line within most MATLAB functions or with logical
% indexing.
 
timestamp = datetime([t,zeros(length(t),1)]);
 
% You can also explicitly specify the import and output formats of your
% date.
We can continue to treat this data as purely tabular, but MATLAB has built-in timetable functionality to make preprocessing and retiming data easier. Convert our regular data table into a timetable, using the datetime vector we made above from combining different columns. To check the proper order of inputs for timetable creation, type help timetable in the command window.
timedData = timetable(timestamp, tab.wind_direction,tab.wind_speed,tab.gust,tab.wave_height,tab.pressure,...
'VariableNames',{'wind_direction';'wind_speed';'gust';'wave_height';'pressure'})
timedData = 3646×5 timetable

Mention cleaning missing, outliers, interpolation
Retime or Resample
% Retime timetable
wtt = retime(timedData(:,[1 2 3 5]),"regular","linear", ...
TimeStep=hours(2));
 
% Retime each override variable to same time vector
TT = retime(timedData(:,"wave_height"),wtt.Properties.RowTimes, ...
"fillwithmissing");
wtt = addvars(wtt,TT.(1),'Before',4, ...
'NewVariableNames',"wave_height");
clear TT

Plot your data

How much info can you fit on a regular plot? Think about your audience and the message you need your figure to convey before creating your visuals!
figure
yyaxis left
scatter(wtt.timestamp,wtt.gust,wtt.pressure./10,wtt.wind_direction,'filled')
 
ylim([0 40])
ylabel('Gust (mph)')
 
yyaxis right
plot(wtt.timestamp,wtt.wind_speed)
ylim([0 40])
ylabel('Wind Speed (mph)')
 
cb = colorbar('location','southoutside');
ylabel(cb, 'Wind Direction')
colormap(cm_infinity)
 
legend('Gust and Pressure','Windspeed')
title(['Rappahannock Light, ',num2str(year(wtt.timestamp(1)))])
Just because you CAN put all of this data in a plot does not mean you SHOULD.
Instead, try creating plots designed to better display the type of data you're analyzing. You can even use animations to show changes to you plots over time.
% Create a plot over time
minwind = ceil(max(wtt.wind_speed));
mpres = ceil(max(wtt.pressure));
lat = 37.538;
lon = -76.014;
 
 
% Setup
f = figure;
 
% Tile 1
ax1 = subplot(2,2,1);
cp1 = compassplot(wtt.wind_direction(1),wtt.wind_speed(1));
colorbar
rlim([0 minwind])
 
 
 
% Tile 2
ax2 = subplot(2,2,2);
p1 = plot(wtt.timestamp(1),wtt.pressure(1));
ylim([1000 mpres+10])
 
 
 
% Tile 3
ax3 = subplot(2,2,[3 4]);
m1 = geoscatter(lat, lon, 100, 'filled');
 
geolimits([37.4 37.6],[-76.6 -75.6])
geobasemap('satellite')
title('Rappahannock Light')
 
% Loop: update plots
for k = 2:numel(wtt.wind_speed)
ax1 = subplot(2,2,1);
cp1 = compassplot(wtt.wind_direction(k),wtt.wind_speed(k));
rlim([0 minwind])
title('Windspeed (mph) & Direction')
 
subplot(2,2,2)
plot(wtt.timestamp(1:k),wtt.pressure(1:k))
ylim([1000 mpres+10])
xlim([wtt.timestamp(1) wtt.timestamp(end)])
title('Pressure (mbar)')
 
%drawnow limitrate % refresh efficiently
pause(0.3) % or use pause for visible slower updates
end
